A. A. Milne.bio: A. A. Milne was an English writer who worked for Punch. He wrote the Pooh stories for his son Christopher Robin. He wrote plays and mysteries as well.

Abbie Farwell Brown.bio: Abbie Farwell Brown was an American author of children's books, many drawn from folklore and myth. She was part of the Boston literary scene. She wrote many books of retold stories.

Adèle Geras.bio: Geras was born Adèle Weston to British Jewish parents and spent her childhood in several countries. She studied at St Hilda's College, Oxford, before becoming a full-time writer. Her first book was Tea at Mrs Manderby's in 1976.

Alan Garner.bio: Alan Garner is an English novelist and folklorist raised in Alderley Edge, whose children's fantasy draws on Cheshire landscape and folklore. He won the 1967 Carnegie Medal for The Owl Service and the 2012 World Fantasy lifetime award. His Stone Book Quartet follows four generations of his family.

Albert Payson Terhune.bio: Albert Payson Terhune was an American author best known for his stories about collies. He raised the dogs at his estate, Sunnybank, in New Jersey. His books about Lad made him famous.

Alexandre Dumas.bio: Alexandre Dumas pere was a French novelist and playwright who began as a dramatist and then turned to serial historical novels. He wrote The Three Musketeers (1844) and The Count of Monte Cristo (1844-46). He founded the Theatre Historique in Paris.
known_for: The Man in the Iron Mask

Alice L. Hopf.bio: Hopf graduated from Vassar in 1927 and wrote children's nature books under the name Alice Hopf. She also wrote science fiction as A. M. Lightner. Two of her nonfiction books won National Science Teachers Association awards.

Allan Baillie.bio: Allan Baillie is an Australian author of children's adventure novels. He worked as a journalist and photographer before writing for young people. Adrift was his first novel for children.

Amy Tan.bio: Tan was born to Chinese immigrant parents and worked as a business writer before turning to fiction. Her debut The Joy Luck Club became a film. She also wrote the children's book The Chinese Siamese Cat.

Ann Nolan Clark.bio: Ann Nolan Clark was an American author who taught at the Tesuque Pueblo school for about 25 years. In 1945 she was sent to Latin America for about five years, which shaped books like Magic Money. She won the 1953 Newbery Medal for Secret of the Andes.

Ann Schlee.bio: Schlee was an English novelist born in the United States who wrote for both children and adults. She studied at Somerville College, Oxford, and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 1997. Her adult novel Rhine Journey was shortlisted for the 1981 Booker Prize.

Anna Sewell.bio: English author who was largely housebound after an injury. She wrote Black Beauty in her final years. It became a landmark of animal welfare.

Anne Lindbergh.bio: Anne Spencer Lindbergh was the daughter of aviators Charles and Anne Morrow Lindbergh and wrote mostly children's novels. She studied at Radcliffe and the Sorbonne and lived in Vermont. She died of cancer in 1993 at age 53.

Anne Sinclair Mehdevi.bio: Mehdevi wrote books about Persia and Iranian life as well as fiction. Open Library lists Persian Adventure (1953), Persia Revisited (1964) and Persian Folk and Fairy Tales (1965). No biographical details could be verified.

Armstrong Sperry.bio: Armstrong Sperry was an author and illustrator who traveled the South Pacific as a young man. He wrote Call It Courage after hearing a Polynesian legend. It won the Newbery Medal in 1941.

Arnold A. Griese.bio: Arnold A. Griese wrote children's fiction about Alaska Native life and also books on education. His titles include At the Mouth of the Luckiest River (1973), Way of Our People (1975) and The Wind Is Not a River (1978). No biographical details were found.
known_for: At the Mouth of the Luckiest River
The Wind Is Not a River

Arthur Bowie Chrisman.bio: American author of folk-tale retellings. He won the first-ever tale Newbery. He farmed in Virginia.

Arthur Conan Doyle.bio: Arthur Conan Doyle was a Scottish-born physician and writer who created Sherlock Holmes. He killed Holmes off in 1893 but later revived him, and also wrote historical fiction and The Lost World. He was knighted in 1902 and later became a spiritualist.

Arthur Roth.bio: Arthur J. Roth wrote The Iceberg Hermit, first published in 1974 by Four Winds Press. Open Library lists several editions of the book under his name. Few personal details could be verified.

Astrid Lindgren.bio: Lindgren grew up on a farm near Vimmerby and worked as a journalist and secretary before becoming an author. She wrote over 30 children's books translated into about 100 languages. She won the Hans Christian Andersen Medal in 1958 and campaigned for children's and animal rights.

Avi.bio: Avi, born Edward Irving Wortis, has written about eighty books for young readers in genres from historical fiction to fantasy and mystery. He won the 2003 Newbery Medal for Crispin: The Cross of Lead. Two of his books, The True Confessions of Charlotte Doyle and Nothing But the Truth, were Newbery Honor books.
known_for: The True Confessions of Charlotte Doyle

B. F. Beebe.bio: B. F. Beebe wrote animal and nature books for young readers, often illustrated by James Ralph Johnson. Goodreads lists 17 works, including African Elephants (1968) and American Wild Horses (1964). No biographical details could be verified.

Barbara Brooks Wallace.bio: Wallace grew up in China and moved to the United States for high school, later graduating from UCLA. Her children's books and mysteries earned two Edgar Awards, for The Twin in the Tavern and Sparrows in the Scullery. Her best-known titles include Peppermints in the Parlor.

Barbara Corcoran.bio: Barbara Corcoran wrote some 72 books, mostly realistic fiction for middle-grade and teen readers, including The Long Journey (1970). Open Library gives her birth year as 1911, and a Montana profile cited in search results calls her a Montana writer. She should not be confused with the real-estate businesswoman of the same name.

Barbara Kingsolver.bio: Kingsolver grew up in rural Kentucky and lived in the Congo as a young child. She studied at DePauw and the University of Arizona. Her fiction deals with social justice and the environment.

Beatrice Culleton.bio: Culleton, who now publishes as Beatrice Culleton Mosionier, grew up in foster homes in Winnipeg. Her novel In Search of April Raintree drew on her own experiences. She has also written children's books and a memoir.

Beatrix Potter.bio: Potter was a writer, illustrator, naturalist and conservationist who studied fungi. She self-published The Tale of Peter Rabbit in 1901. She later farmed in the Lake District and left land to the National Trust.

Bernice G. Anderson.bio: Bernice G. Anderson collected tales from the Otoe people, visiting their reservation near Red Rock, Oklahoma. Her book Indian Sleep-Man Tales was published in 1940. Little else about her life could be confirmed.

Betsy Byars.bio: Betsy Byars was an American children's author who wrote for magazines before her first novel, Clementine, in 1962. She won the 1971 Newbery Medal for Summer of the Swans and a National Book Award for The Night Swimmers. She retired from writing in 1990 per her Wikipedia page.

Betsy Sterman.bio: Betsy Sterman wrote the children's novel Too Much Magic (Lippincott, 1987). Open Library also lists a 1994 edition credited jointly to her and Samuel Sterman. No biographical details could be verified.

Betty K. Erwin.bio: Betty K. Erwin was a physician who began submitting short stories in 1950. She and her husband had six children and lived in Seattle from 1952. Her books are realistic stories drawing on Wisconsin and Seattle.
known_for: Go to the Room of the Eyes

Beverly Cleary.bio: Beverly Cleary was an American author of children's books. A former librarian, she wrote stories of ordinary children after a boy asked her where the books about kids like him were. She was named a Living Legend by the Library of Congress.

Brian Jacques.bio: Jacques worked as a sailor, truck driver, bus driver and milkman before writing. He wrote the first Redwall book for blind children at a Liverpool school where he delivered milk. He hosted a BBC Radio Merseyside show for twenty years.

Bruce Coville.bio: Coville has published over 100 books and worked as a toymaker, gravedigger and teacher before writing. He co-founded Full Cast Audio. He was first published in 1977.
known_for: My Teacher Glows in the Dark

C. S. Lewis.bio: Lewis was a literary scholar who taught at Oxford and later at Cambridge and became a popular Christian writer. He is best known for The Chronicles of Narnia. He was a close friend of J. R. R. Tolkien and a member of the Inklings.

Carlo Collodi.bio: Carlo Collodi was the pen name of Carlo Lorenzini, a journalist and political writer. He serialized Pinocchio in a children's newspaper. The pen name came from his mother's home village.

Carol Fenner.bio: Carol Fenner was a children's author and illustrator. She won a Newbery Honor for Yolonda's Genius.

Carol Ryrie Brink.bio: Brink was raised in Idaho by her grandmother and graduated from UC Berkeley in 1918. She lived in St. Paul, Minnesota, for 42 years and wrote over thirty books. She won the Newbery Medal in 1936.
known_for: Anything Can Happen on the River

Caroline Arnold.bio: Caroline Arnold is an American author of well over 160 nonfiction children's books, mostly on natural and social science. She studied at Grinnell College and the University of Iowa and taught in UCLA Extension's Writers' Program. She made 49 books with photographer Richard Hewett.

Carolyn Sherwin Bailey.bio: Carolyn Sherwin Bailey was an American children's author who began as a teacher and social worker. Her best-known book, Miss Hickory, won the Newbery Medal in 1947. Open Library lists over 80 of her works but no Three Musketeers adaptation.
known_for: Boys and Girls of Colonial Days

Carolyn Sloan.bio: Carolyn Sloan is credited in Open Library with The Sea Child (1987) and several other children's titles. The catalog record seems to merge more than one author with this name, and no reliable biography was found.

Catherine Edwards Sadler.bio: Sadler adapted Sherlock Holmes stories for young readers in the Avon Camelot series starting in 1981. She also wrote Two Chinese Families and Treasure Mountain for Atheneum. No biographical details could be found.

Charles Dickens.bio: Dickens left school at twelve to work in a factory after his father was jailed for debt. He became the leading Victorian novelist, publishing in serial instalments. He also campaigned for social reform.

Charles G. Waugh.bio: American college professor and anthologist who co-edited many anthologies, mostly with Martin H. Greenberg and Isaac Asimov.
known_for: Anthologies with Isaac Asimov and Martin H. Greenberg

Charlotte Brontë.bio: Charlotte Brontë was the eldest of the famous Brontë sisters, who grew up on the Yorkshire moors. She wrote under the pen name Currer Bell. She published Jane Eyre in 1847, to wide acclaim.

Chester Aaron.bio: Chester Aaron was an American writer who also worked as a steelworker, X-ray technician, college professor and garlic farmer. His writing career ran from 1955 to 2011. He studied at UCLA, UC Berkeley and San Francisco State.

Chris Riddell.bio: Riddell is a South African-born English illustrator and political cartoonist for The Observer. He has won three Kate Greenaway Medals and was UK Children's Laureate in 2015. He illustrated The Edge Chronicles, written by Paul Stewart.

Clive King.bio: King read English at Cambridge and served in the Royal Navy in 1943-46. He then worked abroad for the British Council and as a lecturer before writing full-time from 1973. He is best known for Stig of the Dump.

Colby Rodowsky.bio: Rodowsky studied at the College of Notre Dame of Maryland and taught in Baltimore schools. She began writing for children around age forty, and her first novel appeared in 1976. Many of her books follow young protagonists facing hardship.

Collin McDonald.bio: McDonald wrote scary-story collections for young readers published by Cobblehill Books. His books include Nightwaves (1990), The Chilling Hour (1992) and Shadows and Whispers (1994). Other details could not be verified.

Cynthia Rylant.bio: Rylant grew up in West Virginia Appalachian towns and worked as a librarian before writing. She has written picture books and novels.

Cynthia Voigt.bio: Voigt was an English teacher who wrote the Tillerman cycle. She won the Newbery for Dicey's Song.

D. J. Enright.bio: D. J. Enright was an English poet, novelist and critic. He taught in Egypt, Japan, Thailand and Singapore and later directed Chatto and Windus. He received the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry in 1981 and an OBE in 1991.

Daniel Defoe.bio: Daniel Defoe was a merchant, journalist and novelist. He wrote Robinson Crusoe near the end of his life. He is often called a father of the English novel.

Deborah Gangloff.bio: Gangloff wrote the children's book Albert & Victoria, published by Crown in 1989. No biographical details could be found.

Deborah Howe.bio: Deborah Howe was an American author who co-wrote Bunnicula with her husband James. She died young.

Dhan Gopal Mukerji.bio: Mukerji moved to the US to study and became a writer. He wrote about India for American children, and was the first Asian-American Newbery winner.

Diana Wynne Jones.bio: Diana Wynne Jones was a British fantasy writer. She grew up in wartime England. She wrote Howl's Moving Castle.

Dick King-Smith.bio: Dick King-Smith farmed for about twenty years and then became a teacher before turning to writing. His first book, The Fox Busters, appeared in 1978. His best-known book is The Sheep-Pig, which became the film Babe.

Dodie Smith.bio: English novelist and playwright. She wrote 101 Dalmatians. She owned Dalmatians.

Donald J. Sobol.bio: American author of Encyclopedia Brown. He served in WWII. He wrote over 100 books.

Donna Jo Napoli.bio: Napoli is a linguist and author who earned a Harvard degree in 1970 and a PhD in Romance languages in 1973. She teaches at Swarthmore College. Her fiction often retells fairy tales and addresses real-life difficulties.

Doris Gates.bio: Doris Gates was an American librarian and author of children's books. She wrote about California and common people, and her Blue Willow was a Newbery Honor book. She also wrote the Greek myth retellings.

known_for: Incognito Mosquito Takes to the Air

E. B. White.bio: White was a New Yorker essayist and co-author of The Elements of Style. He wrote Charlotte's Web at his farm in Maine, inspired by a spider he watched in his barn.
E. B. White.birthplace: Mount Vernon, New York, United States

E. L. Konigsburg.bio: Konigsburg won two Newbery awards, including for her first book. She trained as a chemist before writing for children and drew on her own family and her daughter's experiences.
known_for: From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler

E. Nesbit.bio: Edith Nesbit wrote humorous fantasy and realistic stories for children with lively real-feeling kids. She was also a socialist and a founder of the Fabian Society. She wrote many books after her family needed money.
known_for: The Story of the Treasure Seekers

E. W. Hildick.bio: Hildick was a British author of many children's books who lived partly in the United States from about 1965. His stories often feature working-class young heroes. He also wrote the science fiction title Manhattan Is Missing.
known_for: The Dragon That Lived Under Manhattan

Edward Eager.bio: Eager was a playwright and lyricist who began writing children's books for his son, inspired by E. Nesbit.

Edward Fenton.bio: This Edward Fenton wrote children's mysteries, including The Phantom of Walkaway Hill and its sequel The Riddle of the Red Whale (Doubleday, 1966). He should not be confused with the Tudor navigator of the same name. No other biographical details could be verified.
known_for: The Riddle of the Red Whale

Eileen Dunlop.bio: Dunlop was head teacher of the Preparatory School of Dollar Academy from 1980 to 1990. She wrote many children's novels set in Scotland, as well as books on Scottish history and folklore. Her birthplace was not listed.

Eleanor Cameron.bio: Eleanor Cameron was a Canadian-American author. She wrote The Wonderful Flight to the Mushroom Planet.
known_for: The Court of the Stone Children
The Wonderful Flight to the Mushroom Planet

Eleanor Coerr.bio: Eleanor Coerr was a Canadian-born American author. She became interested in Sadako's story while working in Japan. She wrote many picture books and chapter books.
known_for: Sadako and the Thousand Paper Cranes

Eleanor Estes.bio: Estes was a children's librarian who began writing while recovering from tuberculosis. Her Connecticut childhood and small-town family life inspired many of her twenty books. She won the Newbery Medal for Ginger Pye.

Eleanor Farjeon.bio: Eleanor Farjeon was an English poet and storyteller who grew up in a literary family. She wrote hymns and fairy tales. The Eleanor Farjeon Award honors her.
known_for: Martin Pippin in the Apple Orchard

Elizabeth Borton de Treviño.bio: Elizabeth Borton de Treviño was an American author and journalist who married a Mexican man and lived in Monterrey, Mexico. She wrote on Mexican and Spanish themes. Her Newbery winner told the story of Juan de Pareja.

Elizabeth Coatsworth.bio: Coatsworth was a poet and author who graduated from Vassar and later lived in Maine. She published over ninety books and married writer Henry Beston in 1929. She won the Newbery Medal for The Cat Who Went to Heaven.
known_for: The Cat Who Went to Heaven

Elizabeth Enright.bio: American author and illustrator from an artistic family. She won the Newbery for Thimble Summer. Her Melendy family books are loved classics.

Elizabeth George Speare.bio: Elizabeth George Speare wrote historical fiction for children after a career teaching high-school English. She won two Newbery Medals, for The Witch of Blackbird Pond and The Bronze Bow. The Sign of the Beaver was a Newbery Honor book.

Elizabeth Janet Gray.bio: Elizabeth Janet Gray, later Vining, was a children's author who won the Newbery Medal for Adam of the Road. She later became tutor to Crown Prince Akihito of Japan.

Elizabeth Yates.bio: Elizabeth Yates was an American author who began as a journalist and settled in New Hampshire. She won the 1951 Newbery Medal for Amos Fortune, Free Man and a 1944 Newbery Honor for Mountain Born. She also wrote a three-volume autobiography.

Ellen Raskin.bio: Raskin was a writer and illustrator who worked about fifteen years as a commercial artist in New York and designed over a thousand book jackets, including the first A Wrinkle in Time. Her mysteries are full of wordplay and visual puzzles. The Westing Game won the 1979 Newbery Medal.
known_for: The Tattooed Potato and Other Clues

Emily Brontë.bio: Emily Brontë was an English novelist and poet, the sister of Charlotte and Anne. She wrote under the name Ellis Bell. Wuthering Heights, her only novel, was published a year before her death.

Enid Bagnold.bio: Enid Bagnold was a British novelist and playwright. She served as a nurse in World War I. National Velvet, her best-known novel, was made into a film with Elizabeth Taylor.

Ernest Hemingway.bio: Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist and short-story writer. He served as an ambulance driver in the First World War and lived in Paris as an expatriate before gaining fame. He won the Pulitzer Prize in 1953 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.
known_for: The Old Man and the Sea

Ernestine N. Byrd.bio: Byrd wrote animal stories for young readers, including The Black Wolf of Savage River (1959), Ice King (1965) and Tor, Wyoming Bighorn (1969). No biographical details could be found.
known_for: The Black Wolf of Savage River

Esther Forbes.bio: American novelist and historian. She won the Pulitzer for history. Johnny Tremain won the Newbery.
known_for: Paul Revere and the World He Lived In

Eth Clifford.bio: Eth Clifford, born Ethel Clifford Rosenberg, was an American writer of children's and young-adult fiction. She began with adult novels under the name Ethel Rosenberg in 1949 and later adopted the Eth Clifford byline. She co-founded David-Stewart Publishing with her husband.
known_for: Help! I'm a Prisoner in the Library!

Florence Atwater.bio: Florence Atwater co-wrote Mr. Popper's Penguins with her husband Richard. The story came from a family joke about penguins. She continued to promote the book after his death.

Florence Parry Heide.bio: Florence Parry Heide began writing after her five children were in school, and her first book appeared in 1967. She wrote more than a hundred books for children and young adults. She is known for the Treehorn series illustrated by Edward Gorey.
known_for: Sound of Sunshine, Sound of Rain

Frances Hodgson Burnett.bio: Frances Hodgson Burnett was a British-American novelist who emigrated as a teenager to Tennessee. She wrote to support her family and became a famed author of children's classics. She loved gardens and cultivated them at her home on Long Island.

Garrison Keillor.bio: American humorist and radio host. He created A Prairie Home Companion. He wrote Lake Wobegon.

Garry Disher.bio: Disher is an Australian author of crime fiction and children's books. His first children's novel, The Bamboo Flute, won a Children's Book Council of Australia award. He is also a three-time winner of the Ned Kelly Award for crime fiction.

Gary Paulsen.bio: Gary Paulsen was an American author of more than 200 books. He was an Iditarod racer. He wrote Hatchet.

Gene DeWeese.bio: DeWeese was an American science fiction writer best known for his Star Trek novels. He also wrote gothic, mystery and young adult fiction, publishing more than forty books. He used several pen names, including Thomas Stratton with Robert Coulson.
known_for: The Adventures of a Two-Minute Werewolf

Gene Stratton-Porter.bio: Gene Stratton-Porter was an American author, photographer and naturalist. She wrote popular novels set in Indiana's Limberlost swamp. She later turned to film production.

Gennady Spirin.bio: Spirin is a Russian painter and children's book illustrator known for his watercolor style. He studied in Moscow and moved to the United States after the Soviet Union dissolved, settling in Princeton, New Jersey. He illustrated many fairy tales and classic stories.

George Selden.bio: George Selden, born George Selden Thompson, was an American children's writer and Yale graduate who studied in Rome on a Fulbright. He is best known for The Cricket in Times Square, a Newbery Honor Book. He also wrote biographies of archaeologists and a 1974 adult novel under the name Terry Andrews.

Gertrude Moderow.bio: Moderow adapted classic novels for young readers, including a David Copperfield published by Scott, Foresman in 1951. No biographical details could be found.

Gian Paolo Ceserani.bio: Italian author who wrote text for illustrated history books for young readers, often with Piero Ventura. His books have been translated into many languages.

H. M. Hoover.bio: Helen Mary Hoover wrote science fiction and other novels mainly for older children from 1969 to 1996. Her stories often explore friendships between people of different generations. She lived for many years in Virginia.

Hans Christian Andersen.bio: Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish author best known for his fairy tales. Born into poverty, he left home as a teenager to pursue a career in Copenhagen's theatre. His stories mix humour, longing and sorrow.

Harold Keith.bio: Keith was an Oklahoma writer who set most of his roughly sixteen books in his home state. He worked for decades as the University of Oklahoma's sports publicist. He won the 1958 Newbery Medal for Rifles for Watie.

Harper Lee.bio: Lee wrote To Kill a Mockingbird, drawing on her Alabama childhood. She was a friend of Truman Capote.

Harriet Beecher Stowe.bio: American author and abolitionist. Her novel galvanized opposition to slavery. She came from a famous preaching family.

Harriett E. Weaver.bio: Harriett Weaver worked as a ranger at Big Basin Redwood Park in California, where she was the only female ranger. Her book Frosty: A Raccoon to Remember tells how she adopted an orphaned raccoon. Her name is sometimes spelled Harriet.

Helen Cresswell.bio: Cresswell wrote more than 100 children's books and scripts for BBC children's television. She is known for comic and supernatural fiction. The Night Watchmen won the Phoenix Award in 1989.

Hilda van Stockum.bio: Van Stockum was a children's author, illustrator and painter who became a US citizen in 1936. She married Ervin Ross Marlin and had six children. She won a Newbery Honor for A Day on Skates.

Honoré Morrow.bio: Honoré Willsie Morrow was an American novelist and magazine editor who edited The Delineator. She focused on fiction after 1919 and is best known for a trilogy about Abraham Lincoln. Her 1926 book On to Oregon! was reissued as Seven Alone.

Howard Pyle.bio: Pyle was an illustrator and author who shaped the look of pirates and knights, and taught N. C. Wyeth.
known_for: The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood
The Story of King Arthur and His Knights

Hugh Lofting.bio: Lofting trained as a civil engineer and served in the Irish Guards in World War I. He created Doctor Dolittle in illustrated letters to his children from the trenches. The Voyages of Doctor Dolittle won the Newbery Medal.

Humphrey Harman.bio: Humphrey Harman wrote on East Africa, collecting folktales from the Lake Victoria region. His Tales Told Near a Crocodile appeared in 1962, followed by More Tales Told Near a Crocodile (1973) and Tales Told to an African King (1978). No biographical details were found.
known_for: More Tales Told Near a Crocodile
Tales Told to an African King

Isaac Bashevis Singer.bio: Isaac Bashevis Singer wrote in Yiddish and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1978. He grew up in a Warsaw rabbi's household and later moved to New York. He began writing for children late in life, with help from his translators.
known_for: Zlateh the Goat and Other Stories

J. K. Rowling.bio: Rowling is a British author best known for the seven-volume Harry Potter series, which has sold hundreds of millions of copies. She also writes crime novels as Robert Galbraith and has written children's books such as The Ickabog.

J. M. Barrie.bio: J. M. Barrie was a Scottish novelist and playwright who made his name with village stories before creating Peter Pan. He was inspired by the Llewelyn Davies boys and gave the Peter Pan copyright to Great Ormond Street Hospital in 1929. He was made a baronet in 1913.

J. R. R. Tolkien.bio: Tolkien was a philologist who held professorships at Oxford. He fought in the First World War and was a close friend of C. S. Lewis. His Middle-earth books made him one of fantasy's defining authors.
J. R. R. Tolkien.birthplace: Bloemfontein, Orange Free State (now South Africa)

Jack London.bio: Jack London was an American novelist and journalist. After working jobs from oyster pirate to Klondike gold prospector, he turned to writing about life on the edge. He became one of the first writers to earn a fortune from fiction.

Jacqueline Balcells.bio: Jacqueline Balcells is a Chilean children's author whose works have been translated into English and French. Open Library lists about 26 works, including El archipiélago de las puntuadas and The Enchanted Raisin (English, 1988). Exact birth details were not found.

James Baldwin.bio: American educator and author of children's retellings. He wrote legends. He worked as a publisher's editor.

James Houston.bio: Houston was an artist, designer and author who worked in the Canadian Arctic. He helped introduce printmaking to the Inuit and later worked as a designer at Steuben Glass. He wrote and illustrated many children's books.

James Howe.bio: James Howe is an American author who wrote the Bunnicula series. His books range from humor to serious issues.

Jan Slepian.bio: Born Janice Berek, Slepian studied psychology and worked as a speech therapist before writing. She wrote children's and young-adult books and poetry. Her book The Alfred Summer features a child with cerebral palsy.

Jane Goodall.bio: Goodall was a primatologist who spent more than six decades studying wild chimpanzees at Gombe Stream in Tanzania, beginning in 1960 under Louis Leakey. Her findings showed that chimpanzees use tools and have complex social lives. She founded the Jane Goodall Institute and the Roots & Shoots youth program.

Jane Langton.bio: Langton studied astronomy and art history and illustrated her own books. She lived in Lincoln, Massachusetts, near Concord, setting many novels there. She received the Edgar Grand Master Award in 2018.

Jane Leslie Conly.bio: Jane Leslie Conly is a children's author and daughter of Robert C. O'Brien. She wrote sequels to her father's work after his death. She also wrote her own novels.
known_for: Racso and the Rats of NIMH
Rasco and the Rats of NIMH

Jane Yolen.bio: Yolen wrote fantasy, science fiction and children's books and earned a BA from Smith College in 1960. She edited books in New York and later lived in Hatfield, Massachusetts. She wrote around 450 books and died in June 2026.

Janet Hickman.bio: Janet Hickman is credited in Open Library with several children's novels from the 1970s to the 2000s. Few personal details could be confirmed.

Janet Taylor Lisle.bio: American author of children's novels. She won a Newbery Honor. She lives in Rhode Island.

Jay Williams.bio: Jay Williams was an American author of books for children and adults, including historical novels. He teamed with Raymond Abrashkin for the Danny Dunn series. He also wrote fantasy and fairy tale picture books.
known_for: Danny Dunn and the Anti-Gravity Paint

Jean Craighead George.bio: George grew up in a family of naturalists and worked as a Washington Post reporter. She wrote more than a hundred books for young readers, often about the natural world. Julie of the Wolves won the Newbery Medal.

Jean Fritz.bio: Jean Fritz was born in China to missionary parents and moved to the US as a teen. She wrote lively, well-researched histories and biographies for children.
known_for: And Then What Happened, Paul Revere?

Jean Merrill.bio: Merrill wrote children's books and worked in publishing. The Pushcart War is her best-known work.

Jerry Spinelli.bio: Spinelli wrote for adults at first, then turned to young readers while raising his children. He won the Newbery Medal for Maniac Magee.

Jill Paton Walsh.bio: Walsh was an English novelist who wrote for children and adults and finished Dorothy Sayers's Lord Peter novels. She was made a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.

Jim Kjelgaard.bio: Jim Kjelgaard grew up on a farm in Pennsylvania's Allegheny Mountains, which shaped his love of the outdoors and dogs. He wrote more than forty novels, mostly about dogs and wild animals. His best-known book is Big Red.

Joan Aiken.bio: Aiken was the daughter of the American poet Conrad Aiken. She wrote more than 100 books, including alternative-history children's novels and thrillers. She was appointed MBE in 1999.

Joan Kahn.bio: Kahn was an editor at Harper & Row from about 1946 to 1980, where she built its mystery list. She edited about eleven suspense anthologies, several for young adults. She received a special Edgar Award in 1989.

Joan W. Blos.bio: American author who also taught. She won the Newbery. She wrote history.

Johanna Spyri.bio: Swiss author whose Heidi has been loved worldwide. She turned to writing in middle age. She drew on Alpine life.

John D. Fitzgerald.bio: Fitzgerald based the Great Brain books on his own boyhood in Utah. He wrote them as a way to tell the stories of his childhood and his clever older brother.

John Steinbeck.bio: American novelist who chronicled California life. He won the Nobel Prize in 1962. He wrote while working odd jobs and was fascinated by marine biology.

Jon Scieszka.bio: Jon Scieszka is a former teacher who writes funny books for kids. He was the first National Ambassador for Young People's Literature and founded the Guys Read project. He is the author of The Stinky Cheese Man.
known_for: The True Story of the 3 Little Pigs

Jonathan Swift.bio: Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish satirist and clergyman who became dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin. He wrote Gulliver's Travels as a biting satire. He also wrote A Modest Proposal.

Joseph Krumgold.bio: Krumgold was a filmmaker who turned to children's novels. He won two Newbery Medals, the first author to do so.
Joseph Krumgold.birthplace: Jersey City, New Jersey, United States

Josephine Poole.bio: Josephine Poole is a pen name of Jane Penelope Josephine Helyar. She published her first book in 1961 and is known for children's and young adult books and television writing. Moon Eyes is one of her best-known works.

Judith Kerr.bio: British author and illustrator who fled Nazi Germany as a child. She wrote about her flight. She also created The Tiger Who Came to Tea.
known_for: The Tiger Who Came to Tea

Judy Blume.bio: Blume began writing while raising her kids. She is known for honest books on growing up and her Fudge stories.
known_for: Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing
Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret

Jules Verne.bio: Verne was a French novelist and playwright. With his publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel he created the Voyages extraordinaires, adventure novels rich in science and geography. He is often called a father of science fiction and is among the most translated authors in the world.
known_for: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas
Around the World in Eighty Days
Journey to the Center of the Earth

Karen Cushman.bio: Karen Cushman was inspired by her studies of medieval history. She wrote historical fiction about girls. She won the Newbery Medal for The Midwife's Apprentice.

Kate Seredy.bio: Seredy trained as an art teacher in Budapest and moved to the United States in 1922. She wrote and illustrated her own books and saw herself first as an illustrator. The White Stag won the Newbery Medal.

Katherine Paterson.bio: American writer born to missionary parents in China. She has won the Newbery twice. She wrote Bridge to Terabithia from her son's grief.

Kathryn A. Minta.bio: Kathryn A. Minta wrote the children's nonfiction book The Digging Badger in 1985. No biographical information could be found online.

Kathryn Lasky.bio: American author of fiction and nonfiction. She wrote Guardians of Ga'Hoole. She writes history too.

Kenneth Grahame.bio: Scottish writer who worked at the Bank of England. He wrote The Wind in the Willows from bedtime stories for his son. He retired early.

L. Frank Baum.bio: L. Frank Baum was an American author who created the Land of Oz. Before writing, he worked as an actor, shopkeeper and journalist. He wrote fourteen Oz novels.

Laura Adams Armer.bio: Armer was a photographer who lived among the Navajo and then wrote about them. She won the Newbery for Waterless Mountain.

Laura Fisher.bio: Laura Fisher is credited with the children's book You Were Princess Last Time (1965) and, in Open Library, Never Try Nathaniel (1968). No biographical details were found, and many unrelated authors share the name.

Laura Ingalls Wilder.bio: Laura Ingalls Wilder was an American writer and former teacher who wrote the Little House books from her pioneer childhood. She began her autobiography Pioneer Girl around 1929, and publishers' rejection led her to rework it into the series. The Laura Ingalls Wilder Medal is named for her.
known_for: Little House in the Big Woods

Lemony Snicket.bio: Lemony Snicket is the pen name and fictional narrator of the American author Daniel Handler. The name came from research for his first book, The Basic Eight. A Series of Unfortunate Events, first published in 1999, has sold over 60 million copies and was adapted for film and television.

Leonard Everett Fisher.bio: Leonard Everett Fisher was an American artist who illustrated about 250 children's books and wrote about 88 of them. He studied at Yale and lived in Westport, Connecticut. He was a finalist for the 2015 NSK Neustadt Prize.

Leonie Kooiker.bio: Kooiker was a Dutch children's writer who also published in the magazine Kris Kras. Her first book, Het malle ding van bobbistiek (1970), won the Gouden Griffel. De heksensteen (1974) appeared in English as The Magic Stone.

Lewis Carroll.bio: Pen name of Charles Dodgson, mathematician and photographer at Oxford. He told Alice stories on a boat trip. He also wrote nonsense poetry.

Linda Sue Park.bio: Korean-American author. She won the Newbery. She was a journalist first.

Lloyd Alexander.bio: Lloyd Alexander was an American novelist, mostly of fantasy for young readers, and wrote 48 books. He won the 1969 Newbery Medal for The High King and National Book Awards for two other titles. He also translated the poet Paul Eluard.

Lois Lenski.bio: Lenski illustrated 57 books by other authors before writing her own. Her regional series portrayed children outside the middle-class mainstream. She won the Newbery Medal for Strawberry Girl.

Lois Lowry.bio: Lois Lowry grew up in a military family and lived in many places. She is known for writing both humorous and serious children's books. She has won two Newbery Medals.

Louisa May Alcott.bio: Louisa May Alcott grew up in a family of philosophers and reformers in Massachusetts. She worked as a nurse in the Civil War and began writing to help support her family. Little Women was based largely on her own sisters.

Louise Fitzhugh.bio: Louise Fitzhugh was an American writer and illustrator. She grew up in Memphis and moved to New York as an adult. Harriet the Spy was her first and most famous book.
known_for: Nobody's Family Is Going to Change

Lynne Reid Banks.bio: British author who first worked as an actress and journalist. She spent years on an Israeli kibbutz. She wrote the Indian in the Cupboard for her sons.

M. M. Kaye.bio: M. M. Kaye was a British writer born in India who started out as a children's book illustrator. She is best known for the bestselling novel The Far Pavilions (1978), and also wrote crime novels and a children's book, The Ordinary Princess. She wrote a three-volume autobiography.

Mabel Leigh Hunt.bio: Hunt grew up in a Quaker household in Indiana and worked as a librarian in Indianapolis from 1926 to 1938. She then wrote full-time, often setting stories in Indiana. Two of her books were Newbery Honor books.

Madeleine L'Engle.bio: American author of fantasy, science fiction and memoirs. A Wrinkle in Time was rejected by many publishers before success. She served as librarian at a New York cathedral.

Maia Wojciechowska.bio: Wojciechowska grew up in Poland, France and England before moving to California in 1942. She wrote children's and young-adult fiction. Shadow of a Bull won the 1965 Newbery Medal.

Mara Kay.bio: Mara Kay wrote young-adult and children's novels published in the 1960s to 1980s. Open Library lists a dozen of her works, including Masha (1968), In Place of Katia (1963) and In Face of Danger (1977). No biographical details were found.

Margaret Mahy.bio: Mahy was a New Zealand librarian who became a prolific children's and young-adult author. She won the Carnegie Medal twice and received the Hans Christian Andersen Award in 2006. Her stories often have supernatural touches but focus on growing up.

Margot Benary-Isbert.bio: Margot Benary-Isbert was a German-American author who emigrated after World War II. She wrote about postwar family life in Germany.

Marguerite Henry.bio: Henry wrote about 59 books, mostly true-based stories about horses and other animals. She often worked with illustrator Wesley Dennis. She won the Newbery Medal for King of the Wind and is also known for Misty of Chincoteague.

Marguerite de Angeli.bio: De Angeli wrote and illustrated more than 30 books, often about families and history. She won the Newbery Medal for The Door in the Wall.

Maria D. Wilkes.bio: Maria D. Wilkes grew up reading the Little House books and became interested in pioneer history. She researched the Caroline Years series using family letters and diaries and consulted the Laura Ingalls Wilder estate. She wrote the series about Caroline Quiner, Laura's mother.

Maria Gripe.bio: Gripe worked as a journalist before becoming a writer, and her husband Harald illustrated most of her books. Her books blend fairy-tale elements with psychological realism. She won the Hans Christian Andersen Medal in 1974.

Marian Potter.bio: Marian Potter wrote the 1982 children's novel A Chance Wild Apple. Little biographical information could be found online. Open Library also lists a picture book under her name, but it could not be confirmed to be the same author.

Marilyn Sachs.bio: American author of realistic children's books. She was a librarian. She wrote about Bronx life.

Marilyn Singer.bio: Singer earned a BA from Queens College and an MA from NYU, then taught high-school English in New York. She began writing in 1974 and has published over one hundred books. Her work spans fiction, nonfiction, poetry and picture books.

Marion Dane Bauer.bio: Marion Dane Bauer is an American children's author who grew up in Oglesby, Illinois, and helped found the MFA in Writing for Children and Young Adults at Vermont College of Fine Arts. Her novel On My Honor was a 1987 Newbery Honor Book. She lives in Saint Paul, Minnesota.

Marion Smoothey.bio: Author of children's mathematics nonfiction in the Let's Investigate series; no personal details found.

Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings.bio: American author who moved to rural Florida. She won the Pulitzer Prize. She wrote of the Florida scrub.

Mark Helprin.bio: Mark Helprin is a novelist and journalist, known for his lyrical fiction. He served in the British merchant navy and the Israeli army. He has also written children's books with Chris Van Allsburg.
known_for: A Soldier of the Great War

Mark Twain.bio: Twain was the pen name of Samuel Clemens, a humorist, journalist, lecturer and former riverboat pilot. Tom Sawyer's town of St. Petersburg is based on Hannibal, Missouri, where he grew up. He is often praised as the greatest American humorist.

Martin H. Greenberg.bio: Martin H. Greenberg was a prolific anthology editor, especially of science fiction and fantasy. He edited or co-edited well over a thousand anthologies. He worked as a university professor before founding a publishing company.

known_for: Tecwyn, the Last of the Welsh Dragons

Mary Stolz.bio: Stolz, born Mary Slattery, began writing in the late 1940s when arthritis kept her housebound. She wrote fiction for children and young adults, mostly for Harper. She earned Newbery Honors for Belling the Tiger and The Noonday Friends.

Maude Casey.bio: Maude Casey wrote Over the Water, first published in England by The Women's Press in 1987 and in the US by Holt in 1994. Open Library lists only two records for her. No further biographical details could be verified.

Meindert DeJong.bio: Meindert DeJong emigrated from the Netherlands to Michigan as a child and published his first book, The Big Goose and the Little White Duck, in 1938. He won the 1955 Newbery Medal for The Wheel on the School and the 1962 Hans Christian Andersen Award. Maurice Sendak illustrated seven of his books.

Michael Bond.bio: Michael Bond was an English author who worked as a BBC cameraman before writing full time in 1965. He is best known for Paddington Bear, which has sold over 35 million copies. He also wrote the Olga da Polga guinea pig books.

Michael Crichton.bio: Crichton was an American author and filmmaker whose techno-thrillers often explored science gone wrong. He earned an MD at Harvard but never practiced. He also directed films such as Westworld and created the television series ER.

Michael Dorris.bio: Dorris was a writer and anthropologist of Modoc descent.
known_for: A Yellow Raft in Blue Water

Michael Ende.bio: Michael Ende was the only child of the painter Edgar Ende, whose work the Nazis labelled degenerate. He worked as an actor and cabaret writer before his first novel in 1960. His books have sold over thirty-five million copies.
known_for: Jim Button and Luke the Engine Driver

Michael Morpurgo.bio: Michael Morpurgo is a British author and former Children's Laureate. He wrote War Horse. He founded Farms for City Children.

Mildred Ames.bio: Mildred Ames wrote young-adult novels, often with a science-fiction angle. Personal details were not verified.
known_for: Without Hats, Who Can Tell the Good Guys

Myron Levoy.bio: Levoy worked as a chemical engineer before becoming a full-time writer. His young-adult books often deal with outsiders, prejudice and identity. He was also active in the peace movement.
known_for: The Magic Hat of Mortimer Wintergreen

Nancy Bond.bio: Nancy Bond is an American writer of children's fantasy. She lived in England for years and drew on her time in Wales. Her Welsh time-slip novel won a Newbery Honor.

Natalie Babbitt.bio: Natalie Babbitt was an American author and illustrator best known for Tuck Everlasting. She illustrated her own books and her husband's. She often explored big questions about life and death in gentle fantasy.

Nathaniel Benchley.bio: Benchley, son of humorist Robert Benchley and father of Peter Benchley, wrote novels and children's books.
known_for: Only Earth and Sky Last Forever

Nina Bawden.bio: Bawden studied at Somerville College, Oxford, and was evacuated to Wales during the war. She wrote for both adults and children. She was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 1987.

Norma Fox Mazer.bio: Mazer grew up in Glens Falls, New York and met her husband, writer Harry Mazer, at Antioch College. She wrote realistic young-adult and children's novels about family and growing up. She also taught in the Vermont College MFA program.
known_for: Mrs. Fish, Ape, and Me, the Dump Queen

Norton Juster.bio: Norton Juster was an American author and architect. He started The Phantom Tollbooth while avoiding work on another project and became a lifelong friend of illustrator Jules Feiffer, who lived upstairs. The book has delighted readers since 1961.

Oliver Butterworth.bio: American children's author and English teacher at Hartford College for Women. He is best known for The Enormous Egg.

P. L. Travers.bio: P. L. Travers was born Helen Lyndon Goff and worked as a dancer and actress. She created Mary Poppins while living in England. She had a rocky relationship with Disney's film.

Pamela Rogers.bio: Rogers wrote The Rare One, a children's novel published by Hamilton and Thomas Nelson in 1973. No biographical details could be found.

Patricia A. McKillip.bio: American fantasy author. She won the World Fantasy Award. She wrote lyrical fantasy.

Patricia Beatty.bio: Patricia Beatty graduated from Reed College and worked as a children's librarian and teacher. She wrote fifty books, ten of them with her first husband, the historian John Beatty. Her Charley Skedaddle won the 1988 Scott O'Dell Award.

Patricia C. McKissack.bio: Patricia McKissack wrote many books on African American history and folklore. She and her husband Fredrick wrote together. She won a Newbery Honor.

Patricia Clapp.bio: American historical novelist. She wrote Constance. She lived long.

known_for: A Tale of Two Cities (simplified adaptation)

Patricia MacLachlan.bio: Patricia MacLachlan was an American children's author who taught English in Connecticut before she began writing in her mid-30s. Her first book, The Sick Day, appeared in 1979. She won the 1986 Newbery Medal for Sarah, Plain and Tall and wrote over 60 children's books.

Patricia Reilly Giff.bio: American author and former teacher. She has written many books. She is known for Lily's Crossing.

Paul Creswick.bio: Paul Creswick was an English author known for his retelling of Robin Hood, later illustrated by N. C. Wyeth. Few biographical details could be verified.

Paul Jennings.bio: Writer of short stories with surprising endings, who emigrated to Australia in 1949. He worked as a speech pathologist before Unreal! (1985), and his stories were adapted for the TV series Round the Twist.

Paul Stewart.bio: Stewart is a British writer of children's, young adult and adult books. He is best known for the three series he wrote with illustrator Chris Riddell, beginning with The Edge Chronicles. Other works include Muddle Earth and the Wyrmeweald trilogy.

Paula Fox.bio: Fox was raised by relatives and caregivers and later taught troubled children. She wrote adult novels, children's books and memoirs. The Slave Dancer won the 1974 Newbery Medal and she won the 1978 Hans Christian Andersen Award.

Pearl S. Buck.bio: Buck grew up in China as the daughter of missionaries. She won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Penelope Farmer.bio: Penelope Farmer is an English children's fantasy writer who studied history at Oxford. Her first children's novel, The Summer Birds, won a Carnegie commendation, and Charlotte Sometimes (1969) is her best known. Her earlier collection The China People appeared in 1960.

Peter Zachary Cohen.bio: Cohen taught English at Kansas State University from 1961 and served on a county planning commission. He studied at the University of Wyoming and served in the US Army from 1954 to 1956. He wrote children's fiction and plays, and lived on a small farm in Alta Vista, Kansas.

Philippa Pearce.bio: Pearce grew up in a mill house in Cambridgeshire, which inspired Tom's Midnight Garden. She worked as a BBC scriptwriter and editor before writing.

Phyllis A. Whitney.bio: Phyllis A. Whitney was an American mystery writer born in Japan to American parents. She wrote 73 novels for adults, young adults and children and was called a Gothic novelist though she preferred 'romantic suspense'. She won Edgar Awards and the Mystery Writers of America Grand Master Award.
known_for: The Mystery of the Haunted Pool
The Mystery of the Hidden Hand

Phyllis Reynolds Naylor.bio: Naylor began writing as a teenager and earned a BA from American University in 1963. She has written over 130 books. She won the Newbery Medal in 1992 for Shiloh.

Piero Ventura.bio: Italian illustrator of historical picture books, often with text by Gian Paolo Ceserani. His book Pompei earned an honorable mention at the 1983 Bratislava biennial.

R. J. Unstead.bio: Robert John Unstead was a teacher who became headmaster of a primary school in Letchworth. He wrote or edited over forty illustrated history books for young readers, some selling in the millions. He served in the RAF in World War II.

Rachel Field.bio: Rachel Field was a poet, novelist and playwright. She won the Newbery Medal for Hitty. She died young at age 47.

Ralph Moody.bio: Rancher, worker and storyteller who wrote about his boyhood in Colorado. He started writing in his fifties after a writing class, and his autobiographies follow his Little Britches years.

Randall Jarrell.bio: Randall Jarrell was an American poet, critic and novelist who also wrote for children. He taught at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro. His children's books were illustrated by Maurice Sendak.

Raymond Abrashkin.bio: Raymond Abrashkin was an American educator and author who co-created the Danny Dunn series with Jay Williams. He taught in a New York school. He died in 1960 while the series was just beginning.
known_for: Danny Dunn and the Anti-Gravity Paint

Richard Adams.bio: Richard Adams worked as a civil servant before publishing Watership Down. He first told the story to his daughters on a car journey. It became a huge success.

Richard Atwater.bio: Richard Atwater was a newspaper columnist and teacher of Greek. He wrote Mr. Popper's Penguins with his wife Florence late in his life. The book was an immediate success.

Roald Dahl.bio: Dahl was a British writer of children's books and short stories, born in Wales to Norwegian parents. He served in the RAF as a fighter pilot and later in intelligence in World War II. His books have sold hundreds of millions of copies.

Robert C. O'Brien.bio: Robert C. O'Brien was the pen name of Robert Leslie Conly, an editor at National Geographic. He wrote Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, which won the Newbery Medal. He died before finishing his last book, which his family completed.
known_for: Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH

Robert Lawson.bio: Robert Lawson was an American author, illustrator and etcher. He illustrated The Story of Ferdinand and Mr. Popper's Penguins and wrote his own books. He is the only person to win both the Caldecott (1941) and Newbery (1945) Medals.

Robert Louis Stevenson.bio: Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, essayist and travel writer who became famous in his own lifetime. His later years were spent in Samoa, where he was called Tusitala, the teller of tales. He is buried on Mount Vaea.
known_for: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

Robert McCloskey.bio: Robert McCloskey was an American author and illustrator known for his careful drawings. He won the Caldecott Medal twice. He studied animals closely, even keeping ducks in his apartment to sketch.

Robert Newman.bio: Robert Newman was an American writer who began his career in radio and also wrote for television. His children's mysteries include The Case of the Baker Street Irregular (1978) and The Case of the Vanishing Corpse (1980). Birthplace comes from a library biography snippet.
known_for: The Case of the Baker Street Irregular
The Case of the Vanishing Corpse

Robert Siegel.bio: Robert Siegel was an American poet and novelist who taught at Dartmouth, Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee. He wrote the children's books Alpha Centauri (1980) and Whalesong (1981), which became a trilogy. He died in South Berwick, Maine.

Robin McKinley.bio: Robin McKinley writes fantasy that often retells fairy tales. She grew up as the daughter of a naval officer and moved often, which made books her constant companion. She also writes about dogs and horses and has lived in England.

Roger Lea MacBride.bio: Roger Lea MacBride was a lawyer, author and political activist who inherited Rose Wilder Lane's literary estate. He was the Libertarian Party's presidential nominee in 1976. He wrote the Rocky Ridge series about Rose Wilder Lane's childhood.

Rose Wilder Lane.bio: Lane was a journalist and the daughter of Laura Ingalls Wilder, whom she helped edit.
Rose Wilder Lane.birthplace: De Smet, Dakota Territory, United States

Rosemary Sutcliff.bio: Rosemary Sutcliff spent much of her childhood in Malta and at naval bases and was a lifelong wheelchair user. She is best known for children's historical fiction. She won the Carnegie Medal in 1959 for The Lantern Bearers.
known_for: The Mark of the Horse Lord

Rosemary Wells.bio: American author and illustrator. She created Max and Ruby. She wrote many books.

Rudyard Kipling.bio: Rudyard Kipling was an English writer born in India. He wrote The Jungle Book and Kim. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

Rumer Godden.bio: Godden grew up in colonial India and ran a dance school in Calcutta for about 20 years. She wrote more than 60 books and nine were filmed. She was made OBE in 1993.

Ruth Manning-Sanders.bio: Ruth Manning-Sanders was a poet and writer who joined a travelling circus as a young woman. In her seventies she began a long series of folk-tale collections, such as A Book of Dragons. She lived in Cornwall.

Ruth Sawyer.bio: Sawyer was a storyteller who collected folk tales and won the Newbery for Roller Skates.

Ruth Stiles Gannett.bio: Gannett wrote My Father's Dragon at age 22 based on stories she heard from her father.

Samuel Sterman.bio: Samuel Sterman is credited with Betsy Sterman on a 1994 edition of Too Much Magic in Open Library. No biographical details could be verified.

Scott O'Dell.bio: O'Dell wrote historical novels after a career as a screenwriter and journalist. He won the Newbery for Island of the Blue Dolphins and set up an award for historical fiction.

Sheila Burnford.bio: Sheila Burnford was born in Scotland and moved to Canada, where she lived in northern Ontario. She wrote The Incredible Journey after her family's pets inspired her. It became a worldwide success.

Sheila Garrigue.bio: Sheila Garrigue wrote novels for young readers. Open Library lists All the Children Were Sent Away (1976), Between Friends (1978) and The Eternal Spring of Mr. Ito (1985). Few personal details could be verified.
known_for: All the Children Were Sent Away
The Eternal Spring of Mr. Ito

Shel Silverstein.bio: Shel Silverstein was an American poet, songwriter and cartoonist. He wrote and illustrated books such as Where the Sidewalk Ends. He also wrote songs such as A Boy Named Sue.

Sid Fleischman.bio: Sid Fleischman began his career as a professional magician and later became a novelist and screenwriter. His comic adventure stories often featured tricks and tall tales. He won the Newbery Medal for The Whipping Boy.

Sonia Levitin.bio: Sonia Levitin was born in Berlin and fled with her family from Nazi Germany as a child. She wrote young-adult and children's books, many drawing on her family's immigrant experience. She went on to write dozens of books.

Stephen Crane.bio: Crane was a journalist and novelist who wrote The Red Badge of Courage without having seen battle. He died young.

Sterling North.bio: Sterling North was a writer, literary editor and author of many books. His best-known work, Rascal, is a memoir of a childhood with a pet raccoon in Wisconsin. He also wrote about rural boyhood.

Susan Cooper.bio: Susan Cooper studied at Somerville College, Oxford, and worked as a reporter for The Sunday Times. She moved to the United States in 1963. She is best known for The Dark Is Rising sequence and won the Newbery Medal for The Grey King.

Susan Dickinson.bio: Dickinson compiled The Usurping Ghost and Other Encounters and Experiences, published by E. P. Dutton in 1971. No biographical details could be found.
known_for: The Usurping Ghost and Other Encounters and Experiences

Suzanne Fisher Staples.bio: Suzanne Fisher Staples is an American author and former journalist. She lived in Pakistan, which inspired Shabanu.

Sylvia Waugh.bio: Sylvia Waugh is a British children's author who worked as a teacher, careers advisor and librarian before turning to writing in 1987. Her first book, The Mennyms (1993), won the Guardian Children's Fiction Prize and led to a five-book series. She later wrote the Ormingat trilogy.

Terry Trueman.bio: Trueman worked as a teacher, counselor and therapist before writing full time. He began as a poet, and his son's cerebral palsy inspired his poetry and Stuck in Neutral. That debut novel earned a Printz Honor in 2001.

Theodora Du Bois.bio: Theodora Du Bois, born Theodora McCormick, wrote mysteries, children's books, romances and science fiction. She married engineer Delafield Du Bois in 1918. Her publisher dropped her after her 1954 novel Seeing Red criticized the House Un-American Activities Committee.

Tom Gilroy.bio: Open Library credits Tom Gilroy with In Bikole: Eight Modern Stories of Life in a West African Village (1978). No biographical details could be verified.

Tove Jansson.bio: Tove Jansson was a Finland-Swedish writer, painter and illustrator from a family of artists. She is best known for the Moomin books, beginning with The Moomins and the Great Flood. She won the Hans Christian Andersen Medal in 1966.

Upton Sinclair.bio: Sinclair was a muckraking novelist and socialist activist who wrote nearly 100 books. The Jungle helped lead to US food-safety laws. He won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1943.

Uri Orlev.bio: Orlev survived the Warsaw Ghetto and Bergen-Belsen as a child and emigrated to Israel after the war. He became a full-time children's writer and translator in 1968. He won the Hans Christian Andersen Award in 1996.
known_for: The Man from the Other Side

Ursula K. Le Guin.bio: Ursula K. Le Guin was an American author of fantasy and science fiction. She wrote the Earthsea books. She won many awards.

Virginia Driving Hawk Sneve.bio: Virginia Driving Hawk Sneve is a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe who grew up on the Rosebud Indian Reservation. She worked as a teacher and school counselor and writes children's books about Native Americans. She received the National Humanities Medal in 2000.

Virginia Hamilton.bio: American author who wrote about African American life and folklore. She won the Newbery Medal. She was the first African American to receive it.

Virginia Sorensen.bio: Sorensen was an American regionalist writer of adult novels and children's books, associated with Mormon-themed fiction. She won the 1957 Newbery Medal for Miracles on Maple Hill. Her children's novels also include Plain Girl and Lotte's Locket.

Walt Morey.bio: Walt Morey was an American author of outdoor stories. He lived in Oregon and Alaska. He is best known for Gentle Ben.

Walter D. Edmonds.bio: Edmonds is best known for historical novels set in upstate New York. Drums Along the Mohawk was a bestseller and a 1939 film. He won the 1942 Newbery Medal for The Matchlock Gun.

Walter Farley.bio: Farley wrote The Black Stallion while a student at Columbia University. It became the first of a long series.

Washington Irving.bio: Washington Irving was an early American author and diplomat. He wrote The Legend of Sleepy Hollow and Rip Van Winkle. He was among the first American writers to earn an international reputation.

Will James.bio: Born Joseph Ernest Nephtali Dufault, he became a cowboy artist and writer and claimed a Montana birth. He won the 1927 Newbery Medal for Smoky the Cowhorse.

William H. Armstrong.bio: Armstrong taught history at Kent School in Connecticut for 52 years and wrote children's books. Sounder won the 1970 Newbery Medal.

William Mayne.bio: English author of children's fiction rooted in Yorkshire. He won the Carnegie Medal. He was a choirboy at Canterbury Cathedral.

William Pène du Bois.bio: Pène du Bois was educated partly in France and wrote and illustrated children's books. He was a founding editor and art editor of The Paris Review. The Twenty-One Balloons won the 1948 Newbery Medal.

William Steig.bio: American cartoonist and children's author. He began children's books in his sixties. He drew for The New Yorker for decades.

William Stevenson.bio: Stevenson was a British-born Canadian journalist and author of nonfiction, fiction and children's books. His bestselling A Man Called Intrepid (1976) became a television miniseries. He also wrote 90 Minutes at Entebbe and the children's novel The Bushbabies.

Willis Lindquist.bio: Lindquist wrote children's books for McGraw-Hill and Whittlesey House, including Burma Boy and Alaska, the Forty-Ninth State. He also adapted Ben-Hur for Scholastic. Biographical details could not be verified.

Willo Davis Roberts.bio: Willo Davis Roberts began with adult mysteries and published her first children's book in 1975. She became known for children's mystery and suspense novels. She won three Edgar Awards.
known_for: The Girl with the Silver Eyes
The View from the Cherry Tree

Wilson Rawls.bio: American author raised in the Ozarks. He burned early manuscripts before rewriting. He wrote Where the Red Fern Grows.

Yoshiko Uchida.bio: Uchida was interned with her family during WWII, an experience that shaped her writing about Japanese Americans.

Zilpha Keatley Snyder.bio: Snyder taught school before publishing her first book in 1964. She wrote 46 books, many of them fantasy and adventure for children. Three of her books were Newbery Honor winners.

a-bear-called-paddington.summary: The Brown family finds a bear from darkest Peru at Paddington Station, and bring him home. His good manners and mishaps lead to funny chaos.
a-bear-called-paddington.title: A Bear Called Paddington

a-book-of-dragons.summary: A collection of dragon tales from around the world, retold in lively language. It includes stories of heroes, princesses and clever tricksters.
a-book-of-dragons.title: A Book of Dragons

a-brand-new-uncle.note: Corrected: published 1961 (Viking), not 1941; it is not part of the Hungarian Good Master stories, so the earlier Kate, Jancsi and Hungary details were wrong.
a-brand-new-uncle.summary: Library catalogs describe a story in which Bard Smith and his wife solve their troubles by taking in a ten-year-old uncle for their grandchildren. It is one of Seredy's last books, which she wrote and illustrated herself.
a-brand-new-uncle.title: A Brand-New Uncle

characters: Maureen — eleven-year-old farm girl who finds the tree
a-chance-wild-apple.note: Published by Morrow, New York, 1982 (library catalog record). Few details online beyond the catalog summary.
a-chance-wild-apple.setting: A Missouri farm during the Great Depression
a-chance-wild-apple.summary: Eleven-year-old Maureen lives on a Missouri farm during the Great Depression. Her luck turns a little when she discovers a special wild apple tree. A quiet rural story of a hard-up family.
a-chance-wild-apple.title: A Chance Wild Apple

a-christmas-carol.summary: Miserly Ebenezer Scrooge is visited by his dead partner and three spirits on Christmas Eve. They show him the cost of his coldness and the warmth he has missed.
a-christmas-carol.title: A Christmas Carol

a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co.summary: A 19th-century American mechanic is knocked out and wakes up in the age of King Arthur. He tries to bring modern ideas to Camelot, with funny and darker consequences.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co.title: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court

a-foot-in-the-grave.note: Publication date varies by source: 1989 in a Goodreads listing, 1990 UK and 1991 US per a bibliography, Kirkus dates the Viking edition Feb 1992. Not the 1987 Bruce Marshall novel of the same title.
a-foot-in-the-grave.summary: A collection of eight ghost and horror tales, each prompted by a strange picture. A grave-robber is dragged into a grave, a ghost-snatcher is snatched and a poisonous aunt comes back as a strangling vine.
a-foot-in-the-grave.title: A Foot in the Grave

a-gathering-of-days.summary: A New Hampshire girl keeps a journal over a year, recording daily life and a family change.
a-gathering-of-days.title: A Gathering of Days

characters: Elnora Comstock — poor, determined young woman
Katharine Comstock — her widowed, bitter mother
Philip Ammon — young man recuperating nearby
Margaret and Wesley Sinton — kind neighbors
a-girl-of-the-limberlost.note: Source URL was the disambiguation title; corrected. Added neighbors; mother's name Katharine.
a-girl-of-the-limberlost.setting: Limberlost Swamp and the town of Onabasha, northeastern Indiana, early 1900s
a-girl-of-the-limberlost.summary: Elnora Comstock grows up poor beside the Limberlost swamp in Indiana, with a mother who resents her. She pays for her schooling by collecting and selling moths and other swamp specimens, and finds a calling in nature.
a-girl-of-the-limberlost.title: A Girl of the Limberlost

a-grass-rope.summary: In a Yorkshire village, children seek a unicorn that legend says only a maiden can lure. A hunt for treasure follows.
a-grass-rope.title: A Grass Rope

characters: David — the boy (age given as 12 or 13 by different sources)
Sarah Tierney — elderly widow devoted to her horse
a-kingdom-in-a-horse.note: Earlier draft said the boy tries to help a stolen horse; that does not match catalog and review descriptions. Boy's age varies by source.
a-kingdom-in-a-horse.summary: A boy's father, a former rodeo clown, retires to Vermont and tries to buy his son a horse, but the horse ends up with an elderly widow. The mare, Gypsy, gradually draws the boy, his father and the widow together.
a-kingdom-in-a-horse.title: A Kingdom in a Horse

a-little-princess.summary: Sara Crewe, a rich and imaginative schoolgirl, is reduced to servitude when her father dies. She keeps her dignity through stories and kindness.
a-little-princess.title: A Little Princess

a-long-vacation.note: Notebook title 'A Long Vacation' corrected to the standard English title Two Years' Vacation (French: Deux ans de vacances; also Adrift in the Pacific). Draft character names Doniphan and Jacques were not confirmed on the page and were dropped.
a-long-vacation.setting: Auckland, New Zealand, then an uncharted island in the South Pacific, 1860
a-long-vacation.summary: A party of schoolboys aged eight to fourteen drifts out to sea from Auckland when their schooner breaks its moorings in a storm. They are wrecked on an uncharted island and must organize themselves to survive there for two years.
a-long-vacation.title: Two Years' Vacation

a-newbery-halloween.summary: An anthology of Halloween stories by Newbery-winning authors. It collects spooky and funny tales.
a-newbery-halloween.title: A Newbery Halloween

characters: Sunny Baudelaire — baby with sharp teeth
a-series-of-unfortunate-events-the-bad-b.note: Transcribed as 'A Series of Unfortunate Events: The Bad Beginning'; Book the First. Lemony Snicket is the pen name of Daniel Handler. First published by HarperCollins, 30 September 1999.
a-series-of-unfortunate-events-the-bad-b.setting: Briny Beach and Count Olaf's run-down house
a-series-of-unfortunate-events-the-bad-b.summary: After a fire kills their parents, the three Baudelaire children are sent to live with a distant relative, Count Olaf. He is only interested in their inherited fortune and treats them cruelly while he schemes. The children must rely on their own talents to stay one step ahead of him.
a-series-of-unfortunate-events-the-bad-b.title: The Bad Beginning

a-single-shard.summary: Orphan Tree-ear dreams of becoming a potter in 12th-century Korea.
a-single-shard.title: A Single Shard

a-string-in-the-harp.summary: After their mother's death, the Jones family moves to Wales where Peter, twelve, finds an ancient harp tuning key that takes him back to the time of the bard Taliesin.
a-string-in-the-harp.title: A String in the Harp

a-swiftly-tilting-planet.setting: Time travel across New England and Wales
a-swiftly-tilting-planet.summary: Charles Wallace, riding a unicorn, travels through time to prevent a world-ending catastrophe. He must change events in the past.
a-swiftly-tilting-planet.title: A Swiftly Tilting Planet

a-tale-of-two-cities.summary: Set in London and Paris during the French Revolution, the novel follows a physician freed from prison, his daughter, and two men whose fates cross. It is about sacrifice, resurrection and the price of revolution.
a-tale-of-two-cities.title: A Tale of Two Cities

a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.note: Original novel 1859. The adapted edition by Patricia Krapesh (also spelled Patti) was a 1991 Steck-Vaughn easy reader according to a library catalog record seen in search results; no page describing the adaptation itself could be opened.
a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.summary: In this simplified retelling of Dickens's novel, a freed Bastille prisoner, his daughter and a French exile are drawn into the dangers of London and Paris before and during the French Revolution. A London lawyer who closely resembles the exile plays a decisive part.
a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.title: A Tale of Two Cities

characters: Twin brother and sister — the central pair
a-trick-of-light.note: The earlier draft described a mystery about a family move; the catalog description is about twins growing apart. Atheneum, 1972, 117 pages.
a-trick-of-light.summary: A twin brother and sister discover that the closeness of their childhood must change if they are to grow up. A short, emotional novel for young readers.
a-trick-of-light.title: A Trick of Light

a-whisper-in-the-night.summary: A collection of spooky and suspenseful tales that blend the eerie with Aiken's dry humor. Ideal for read-aloud on a dark evening.
a-whisper-in-the-night.title: A Whisper in the Night: Tales of Terror and Suspense

a-wind-in-the-door.setting: Murry home and the inner world of a cell
a-wind-in-the-door.summary: Charles Wallace is ill, and Meg must journey inside his body at the tiniest scale. Some surprising helpers aid her.
a-wind-in-the-door.title: A Wind in the Door

a-wrinkle-in-time.setting: Earth and other planets, mid-20th century
a-wrinkle-in-time.summary: Meg Murry and her brother set out across the universe to find her missing father. Three odd guides help in the fight against a dark force.
a-wrinkle-in-time.title: A Wrinkle in Time

abel-s-island.summary: A pampered mouse is swept away by a storm and trapped on a river island. He learns resourcefulness over a year.
abel-s-island.title: Abel's Island

adam-of-the-road.summary: Adam, an eleven-year-old minstrel's son, is separated from his father and dog in 13th-century England and searches the roads to find them.
adam-of-the-road.title: Adam of the Road

adrift.summary: Flynn and his sister Sally are carried out to sea on a makeshift raft in a story of survival at sea.
adrift.title: Adrift

characters: Jim — escaped slave and Huck's companion
The King and the Duke — con men
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn.note: First published in the UK and Canada in December 1884; US edition February 1885. Contains racial slurs and portrayals; best read with discussion.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn.summary: Huck fakes his own death to escape his abusive father and drifts down the Mississippi on a raft with Jim, who has run away from slavery. They meet feuding families and swindlers while Huck wrestles with what he has been taught about right and wrong.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

afternoon-of-the-elves.summary: Hillary visits a strange girl's backyard and glimpses a tiny elf village.
afternoon-of-the-elves.title: Afternoon of the Elves

albert-and-victoria.note: Earlier draft treated this as a book about Queen Victoria and Prince Albert; Open Library lists Gangloff's Albert & Victoria (Crown, 1989) with subjects Insects and Friendship. Plot details not otherwise verified.
albert-and-victoria.summary: A children's book published by Crown in 1989 in which the title characters are insects. Library subject headings list it under friendship and insects, not royal history.
albert-and-victoria.title: Albert & Victoria

alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland.summary: Alice follows a White Rabbit down a hole into a world of nonsense and strange characters.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

all-the-children-were-sent-away.note: Year (1976) confirmed by Open Library; plot description comes from a library catalog record (Bradbury Press, Scarsdale NY, 171 pp.) seen in a search result. Draft details about evacuation from London were not confirmed.
all-the-children-were-sent-away.setting: Britain and Canada during World War II
all-the-children-were-sent-away.summary: A World War II novel about an eight-year-old British girl who is among the many children sent overseas to Canada. It centers on her fear and sense of isolation far from home.
all-the-children-were-sent-away.title: All the Children Were Sent Away

characters: Little Red Hen — small, tough, wary
along-came-a-dog.summary: A lonely stray dog finds a home on a farm and takes it upon himself to protect a small red hen from a hungry hawk. It's a tender story of devotion between unlikely friends.
along-came-a-dog.title: Along Came a Dog

characters: Becky — girl who travels back in time
alpha-centauri.note: Draft described a girl named Alpha Centauri in a fantasy world; the catalog record instead gives the heroine as Becky. Author is the poet and novelist Robert Siegel (1939-2012), whose Wikipedia page lists Alpha Centauri (1980).
alpha-centauri.setting: A farm in England and ancient Britain
alpha-centauri.summary: A girl named Becky, visiting a farm in England, is carried back to ancient Britain. There she finds cruel men trying to wipe out a peaceful race of centaurs.
alpha-centauri.title: Alpha Centauri

amos-fortune-free-man.summary: Born an African prince, Amos Fortune is captured and enslaved in Massachusetts, and eventually buys his freedom. He settles in New Hampshire and helps others to freedom.
amos-fortune-free-man.title: Amos Fortune, Free Man

amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.note: Existence confirmed in Open Library (1964, Holt, Rinehart and Winston; author also listed as Laura H. Fisher). Plot not verified; the earlier horse-story description was a guess.
amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.summary: A children's book published in 1964 by Holt, Rinehart and Winston. No plot description could be found online.
amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.title: Amy and the Sorrel Summer

an-american-ghost.note: Plot not verified; reprinted by Zumaya Publications in 2011.
an-american-ghost.summary: A young adult novel by Chester Aaron, published by Harcourt in 1973. Details of the plot could not be confirmed online.
an-american-ghost.title: An American Ghost

anastasia-again.summary: The Krupniks move from Cambridge to the suburbs, and Anastasia hates it at first. She sets out to make the best of her new home.
anastasia-again.title: Anastasia Again!

anastasia-krupnik.summary: Ten-year-old Anastasia keeps lists of what she loves and hates, and struggles with a big change: her parents are expecting a baby. Funny and honest about growing up.
anastasia-krupnik.title: Anastasia Krupnik

and-now-miguel.summary: Miguel, a New Mexico sheepherder's son, wants to go with the men to the Sangre de Cristo mountains. He must learn what that means.
and-now-miguel.title: ...And Now Miguel

anna-to-the-infinite-power.summary: Anna is a gifted girl who discovers she has been cloned. She meets her duplicates and faces questions about identity.
anna-to-the-infinite-power.title: Anna to the Infinite Power

another-heaven-another-earth.summary: A group of colonists on a distant planet face a harsh new world and their own beliefs. The story is a thoughtful tale of survival.
another-heaven-another-earth.title: Another Heaven, Another Earth

apricots-at-midnight.note: Full title is Apricots at Midnight and Other Stories from a Patchwork Quilt; first published by Hamish Hamilton in 1977, US edition Atheneum 1982.
apricots-at-midnight.summary: Aunt Pinny tells stories drawn from the scraps of an old patchwork quilt. Each patch, such as a red velvet dress or a haunted lace one, opens onto a tale.
apricots-at-midnight.title: Apricots at Midnight

characters: April Raintree — older sister, light-skinned, tries to leave her heritage behind
Cheryl Raintree — younger sister, proud of her Metis heritage
april-raintree.note: Notebook says 'April Raintree', the 1984 expurgated edition for young readers; the original 1983 novel is In Search of April Raintree. Author now publishes as Beatrice Culleton Mosionier. Subject matter is mature.
april-raintree.summary: Two Metis sisters, April and Cheryl Raintree, are taken from their family in Manitoba and raised in separate foster homes. As adults one embraces her Metis identity while the other tries to leave it behind.
april-raintree.title: In Search of April Raintree

awards: Boston Globe-Horn Book Honor Book for Fiction (1982)
ask-me-no-questions.note: Date conflict: Bookroo says first published 1976 (Macmillan, London); Wikipedia's Ann Schlee page lists it as 1979. Setting period (Victorian) not confirmed. A different novel with the same title (Marina Budhos, 2006) exists.
ask-me-no-questions.setting: Their aunt's house, away from an epidemic
